title: Stewart v. Rosenblum
description: Whether the Pretrial Fairness Act, by limiting a judge's ability to indefinitely detain defendants, violates the separation of powers clause of the Illinois Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioner argued that the Pretrial Fairness Act is constitutional and the circuit court lacked statutory authority to indefinitely detain her, as she was not charged with a detainable offense and did not qualify for indefinite detention under the Act.
defendant_argument: The respondent judge argued that sections 110-6 and 110-6.1 of the Act were unconstitutional as applied to the petitioner's case because they unduly infringed on his inherent judicial authority to administer justice, control his docket, and manage proceedings, especially when a defendant repeatedly fails to appear.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the circuit court's judgment, finding that sections 110-6 and 110-6.1 of the Pretrial Fairness Act are constitutional as applied to the petitioner's case, and ordered her immediate release from custody.

title: State v. Spencer
description: Whether Eugene Spencer's 100-year aggregate sentence, with eligibility for parole after 20 years, constitutes a de facto life sentence that violates the Illinois proportionate penalties clause for an emerging adult.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that Spencer's 100-year sentence is not a de facto life sentence because he is eligible for parole after serving 20 years, and the youth parole statute (730 ILCS 5/5-4.5-115(b)) provides a meaningful opportunity for release.
defendant_argument: Spencer argued that his 100-year sentence is a de facto life sentence that violates the Illinois proportionate penalties clause because it was imposed without sufficient consideration of youth-related factors, and the parole statute does not provide a meaningful opportunity for parole.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the appellate court's judgment that Spencer's sentence is not a de facto life sentence, but clarified that he is not precluded from bringing an as-applied challenge to his sentence under the proportionate penalties clause in a postconviction proceeding.

title: McCombie v. Illinois State Board of Elections
description: Whether the plaintiffs' motion to challenge the 2021 legislative redistricting plan, alleging it violates constitutional requirements for compact districts and political fairness, is timely or barred by the equitable doctrine of laches.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argue their motion is timely, relying on federal and out-of-state case law, and that the 2021 Enacted Plan violates the Illinois Constitution by featuring gerrymandered districts for partisan purposes and lacking compactness.
defendant_argument: The defendants argue that the plaintiffs' motion is untimely and barred by the doctrine of laches because it was filed more than three years and two election cycles after the redistricting map was enacted.
decision_outcome: The court denied the plaintiffs' motion for leave to file a complaint for declaratory judgment and injunctive relief, ruling it was untimely and barred by laches.

title: People v. Hagestedt
description: Whether police officers' actions of using a flashlight and an angled view to peer into a chained and locked, slightly ajar kitchen cabinet during a gas leak investigation constituted an unreasonable warrantless search in violation of the Fourth Amendment.
plaintiff_argument: The police officers exceeded the scope of their authorized entry (gas leak investigation) and conducted an unreasonable warrantless search by using a flashlight to peer into a chained and locked cabinet, whose contents were not in plain view, thereby violating his Fourth Amendment rights.
defendant_argument: The officers' actions did not constitute a search because the contents were openly or plainly visible, and the use of a flashlight to illuminate a darkened area does not transform an observation into a search. The defendant also failed to prove a reasonable expectation of privacy.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the lower courts' judgments, ruling that the trial court erred in denying the defendant's motion to suppress evidence, and vacated the defendant's conviction and sentence.

title: People v. White
description: Whether Sedrick White's 40-year sentence for first-degree murder, imposed when he was 20 years old, violates the proportionate penalties clause of the Illinois Constitution and the Eighth Amendment, given his youth and rehabilitative potential.
plaintiff_argument: Sedrick White argued that his 40-year sentence constituted a de facto life sentence, violating constitutional protections due to the court's failure to adequately consider his youth and rehabilitative potential, and that his blind guilty plea did not waive this challenge.
defendant_argument: The State argued that White's 40-year sentence was proportionate to the offense and did not shock the moral sense of the community, and that the circuit court properly considered all relevant factors, including his age, conceding that an open guilty plea does not waive sentencing errors.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the appellate court's judgment, finding that Sedrick White's 40-year sentence for first-degree murder did not violate the proportionate penalties clause of the Illinois Constitution.

title: Martin v. Goodrich Corporation
description: Whether section 1(f) of the Workers' Occupational Diseases Act is a statute of repose, whether section 1.1 applies prospectively, and whether this prospective application violates Illinois's due process guarantee.
plaintiff_argument: Candice Martin argued that section 1(f) is a statute of repose, allowing her claim under section 1.1, and that applying section 1.1 prospectively to cases filed after the amendment, even if the exposure occurred earlier, does not violate due process.
defendant_argument: Goodrich Corporation argued that section 1(f) is not a statute of repose, meaning section 1.1 would not apply, and that applying section 1.1 to revive claims where the defendant had a vested right to a defense would violate due process.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that section 1(f) is a statute of repose, section 1.1 applies prospectively under section 4 of the Statute on Statutes, and this prospective application does not offend Illinois's due process guarantee, thereby allowing the plaintiff's civil action to proceed.

title: People v. Clark
description: Whether an arrest based on an investigative alert without a warrant violates the Illinois Constitution, and whether the sentencing of a juvenile offender must explicitly consider specific statutory mitigating factors.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that warrantless arrests based on probable cause are constitutional under both federal and Illinois law, and that the circuit court adequately considered the relevant factors for sentencing, even if not explicitly reciting each one, and that the juvenile sentencing provisions did not apply retroactively.
defendant_argument: Clark argued his arrest was unconstitutional because it was based on an investigative alert without a warrant, violating the Fourth Amendment and Article I, Section 6 of the Illinois Constitution. He also argued the circuit court improperly sentenced him by failing to make specific findings pursuant to section 5-4.5-105(a) of the Code, which applies to juvenile offenders.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the appellate court's judgment, upholding the defendant's convictions and sentence.

title: Walker v. Chasteen
description: Whether the circuit court has subject-matter jurisdiction to order refunds of unconstitutional filing fees, or if such claims must be brought in the Court of Claims under sovereign immunity principles.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the officer-suit exception to sovereign immunity applies to both their claim for injunctive relief and their claim for refunds, asserting that the refund claim is inextricably tied to the injunctive relief and thus the circuit court should decide both.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the officer-suit exception only applied to the claim for prospective injunctive relief, and once the unconstitutional statutes were enjoined, the refund claim became a present claim against the State for a past wrong, which falls under the exclusive jurisdiction of the Court of Claims due to sovereign immunity.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the appellate court's judgment and affirmed the circuit court's dismissal of the plaintiffs' refund claim, holding that the circuit court lacked jurisdiction over the refund claim due to sovereign immunity.

title: Arlington Heights Pension Fund v. Pritzker
description: Whether Public Act 101-610, which consolidated local police and firefighter pension fund assets into statewide funds, violates the pension protection clause or the takings clause of the Illinois Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The Act diminishes and impairs pension benefits by diluting voting power, affecting investment control, imposing transition costs, and constitutes a taking of private property by requiring the transfer of fund assets and bearing associated costs.
defendant_argument: The Act does not violate the pension protection clause because it does not affect the value of monetary pension benefits, and the takings clause is inapplicable as it concerns real property, not the management of fund assets.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the appellate court's judgment, which upheld the circuit court's decision to grant summary judgment in favor of the defendants, finding that the Act did not violate the pension protection clause or the takings clause.

title: Caulkins v. Pritzker
description: Whether the Protect Illinois Communities Act, which restricts assault weapons and large capacity magazines, violates the Illinois Constitution's equal protection and special legislation clauses due to its exemptions, and whether the Act was passed in violation of the three-readings requirement.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the Act's exemptions for certain professionals and grandfathered individuals deny law-abiding citizens equal protection and constitute special legislation, and that the Act violates the three-readings requirement of the Illinois Constitution.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the Act's exemptions do not deny equal protection or constitute special legislation because the plaintiffs are not similarly situated to the exempt classes, and that the plaintiffs waived their second amendment and three-readings claims.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the circuit court's judgment, ruling that the Act's exemptions do not violate equal protection or special legislation, and that the plaintiffs waived their second amendment challenge and were jurisdictionally barred from renewing their three-readings claim.

title: Rowe v. Raoul
description: Whether Public Acts 101-652 and 102-1104 (SAFE-T Act), which abolished monetary bail and revised pretrial release provisions, violate the Illinois Constitution's bail clause, crime victims' rights clause, and separation of powers clause.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the Act's pretrial release provisions violated the Illinois Constitution's bail clause, crime victims' rights clause, and separation of powers clause, contending that eliminating monetary bail was an improper constitutional amendment, stripped courts of authority, and prevented the protection of victims' safety.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the Act was constitutional, asserting that the bail clause does not mandate monetary bail, the Act's provisions adequately consider crime victims' rights, and the legislature has the authority to regulate the bail system without violating separation of powers.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the circuit court's decision, ruling that the Public Acts 101-652 and 102-1104 (SAFE-T Act) are constitutional and do not violate the Illinois Constitution.

title: People v. Mayfield
description: Whether the Illinois Supreme Court's emergency administrative orders, which tolled the speedy-trial statute during COVID-19, violated the separation-of-powers clause of the Illinois Constitution by infringing on the General Assembly's legislative authority.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the court's administrative orders were a valid exercise of its general administrative and supervisory authority over all state courts, and therefore prevailed over the conflicting speedy-trial statute.
defendant_argument: Gary Mayfield argued that the circuit court's noncompliance with the speedy-trial statute compelled reversal of his conviction because the supreme court's administrative orders violated the Illinois Constitution's separation-of-powers clause.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the defendant's conviction, holding that its emergency orders tolling the speedy-trial statute did not violate the separation-of-powers clause.

title: People v. Brown
description: Whether defendant Servetus Brown received ineffective assistance of trial counsel because his attorney agreed to a process where juror challenges were exercised off the record and outside his presence, with the plaintiff arguing counsel was effective and the defendant arguing counsel was ineffective.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff (State) argued that the defendant's counsel provided adequate assistance and that the defendant failed to demonstrate prejudice from the jury selection process.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that his trial counsel was ineffective for failing to object to the off-the-record sidebar conferences for juror challenges held in his absence, which he claimed violated his constitutional right to be present at a critical stage of trial, and that prejudice should be presumed.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgment of the appellate court, which had affirmed the circuit court's judgment, thereby upholding the defendant's conviction.

title: Illinois Road & Transportation Builders Association v. The County of Cook
description: Whether the 2016 transportation taxes and fees lockbox amendment to the Illinois Constitution applies to transportation-related revenues generated by home-rule units, or if it is limited to state-imposed tax revenues.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argue that the Amendment's plain language, particularly subsection (a), broadly applies to all transportation-related revenues, including those from home-rule units, and that no explicit exemption for home-rule units was created, unlike for federal funds.
defendant_argument: The County argues that the Amendment, when read as a whole and considering references to 'laws' and 'statute,' applies exclusively to state-imposed tax revenues and not to revenues generated by home-rule units under their constitutional home-rule spending authority.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the circuit court's dismissal of the plaintiffs' complaint, finding that the plaintiffs had associational standing and that the Cook County Transportation Taxes are subject to the Amendment, remanding the case for further proceedings.

title: People v. Moon
description: Whether a criminal defendant's trial before an unsworn jury requires automatic reversal without a showing of prejudice to the defendant, with the defendant arguing for automatic reversal and the plaintiff arguing against it without a showing of prejudice.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the defendant forfeited the error by not objecting at trial, and even if it was an error, it was harmless and did not constitute plain error requiring automatic reversal without a showing of prejudice.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the circuit court's failure to administer a trial oath to the jury was a "clear error" and a structural error, requiring automatic reversal regardless of the strength of the evidence or any showing of prejudice.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the appellate and circuit courts' judgments, the defendant's conviction and sentence, and remanded the case for a new trial, concluding that the complete failure to swear the jury with a trial oath was structural error.

title: International Association of Fire Fighters, Local 50 v. The City of Peoria
description: Whether the City of Peoria's ordinance defining "catastrophic injury" and "injury" for public safety employee benefits is a valid exercise of its home rule authority or is preempted by the Illinois Public Safety Employee Benefits Act and judicial precedent.
plaintiff_argument: The Union argued that the City's ordinance improperly redefined "catastrophic injury" and "injury" in a way that is inconsistent with the Public Safety Employee Benefits Act and established judicial interpretations, thus exceeding its home rule authority and being preempted.
defendant_argument: The City argued it has home rule authority to define "catastrophic injury" and "injury" for itself, and that prior judicial interpretations of the Act do not automatically become part of the statute unless explicitly adopted by the General Assembly.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower court's grant of summary judgment in favor of the Union, finding the City's ordinance invalid because its definitions were inconsistent with the Act and therefore preempted.

title: People v. House
description: Whether Antonio House's mandatory natural life sentence for murders committed at age 19 violates the proportionate penalties clause of the Illinois Constitution, and whether his actual innocence claim warrants further review.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the appellate court erroneously considered the as-applied proportionate penalties claim without a sufficiently developed evidentiary record, and that the mandatory life sentence for an adult offender is constitutional. They also agreed to remand the actual innocence claim for reconsideration in light of new precedent.
defendant_argument: House argued that his mandatory natural life sentence was unconstitutional as applied to him under the proportionate penalties clause, citing evolving science on juvenile maturity and brain development that should extend Miller v. Alabama protections to young adults aged 18-21. He also argued for cross-relief on his actual innocence claim based on newly discovered evidence.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the appellate court's finding that the petitioner's sentence violated the proportionate penalties clause and vacated the appellate court's judgment affirming the dismissal of the petitioner's actual innocence claim, remanding the entire cause to the circuit court for further second-stage postconviction proceedings on both issues.

title: Guns Save Life, Inc. v. Ali
description: Whether Cook County's tax ordinances on the retail purchase of firearms and ammunition violate the uniformity clause of the Illinois Constitution by burdening the fundamental right to bear arms.
plaintiff_argument: The taxes violate the uniformity clause of the Illinois Constitution and unconstitutionally burden the fundamental right to keep and bear arms for self-defense.
defendant_argument: The taxes are a proper exercise of home rule taxing powers, do not meaningfully impede the right to bear arms, and are substantially related to the important governmental interest of public safety.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that Cook County's firearm and ammunition tax ordinances are unconstitutional under the uniformity clause of the Illinois Constitution, reversing the appellate court's judgment in part and remanding for summary judgment in favor of the plaintiffs.

title: People v. McCavitt
description: Whether the police violated the Fourth Amendment by searching the defendant's computer for child pornography after his acquittal on sexual assault charges, using data previously seized under a warrant that also covered unauthorized video recording, without obtaining a new warrant.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the search for child pornography was lawful because the original warrant authorized a search for unauthorized video recording, which was not resolved by the sexual assault acquittal, and the child pornography was discovered in plain view during a search reasonably directed at that authorized purpose.
defendant_argument: McCavitt argued that his acquittal for sexual assault restored his expectation of privacy in his computer data, making any subsequent search without a new warrant unlawful and a violation of his Fourth Amendment rights, especially given the delay in the search.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the appellate court's judgment, affirming the trial court's denial of the defendant's motion to suppress the child pornography evidence.

title: People v. Bochenek
description: Whether the statutory venue provision for identity theft, which allows for proper venue where the victim resides, satisfies the constitutional mandate that a defendant shall be tried in the county where the offense is alleged to have been committed.
plaintiff_argument: The People argue that the venue provision is constitutional because the offense of identity theft can be deemed committed where the victim's personal identifying information is 'located' at their residence, satisfying the constitutional requirement.
defendant_argument: Dominik K. Bochenek argues that the venue provision is unconstitutional because the victim's residence is an arbitrary location unrelated to where the physical acts of the offense occurred.
decision_outcome: The court held that the venue provision allowing for trial in the county where the victim resides is constitutional and affirmed the appellate court's judgment.

title: People v. Bass
description: Whether a routine traffic stop was unlawfully prolonged by running a name check on a passenger, violating the Fourth Amendment, and whether arrests based on investigative alerts, even with probable cause, violate the Illinois Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued the traffic stop was lawfully executed and not unlawfully prolonged, and that investigative alerts are constitutional under both the United States and Illinois Constitutions.
defendant_argument: Bass argued the traffic stop was unlawfully extended by running a name check unrelated to the red light violation, and that investigative alerts are unconstitutional under Article I, Section 6 of the Illinois Constitution.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the appellate court's decision to reverse Bass's conviction and remand for a new trial due to an unlawfully prolonged traffic stop, but vacated the appellate court's portions dealing with limited lockstep analysis and investigatory alerts.
